## Continous data Either a gradient or two diverging colours. My preference for most charts is one colour from opaque to low opacity. As shown below, when you run from one colour to another the results are often hard to follow. The exception perhaps are maps, where a third middle colour, that can be white, works quite well. This does not work for something like a dot plot. ```{r} base <- ggplot(mpg, aes(cyl, displ, colour = displ)) + geom_point(size = 2) base + scale_color_gradient(low = ncolours$colours_diverge_mint[1], high = ncolours$colours_diverge_mint[2]) ```
## Categorical data. ### Different categorical colours. ```{r} species <- penguin %>% group_by(species) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>% mutate(species_percent = 100 * (n/ sum(n))) bar1 <- species %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = species_percent, fill = species)) + geom_col() + scale_fill_manual(values = ncolours$colours10) bar1 ```
### One colour ```{r} island <- penguin %>% group_by(island) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>% mutate(island_percent = 100 * (n/ sum(n))) bar2 <- island %>% ggplot(aes(x = island, y = island_percent)) + geom_col(fill = ncolours$blue3) bar2 ```
### Lots of colours ```{r} penguin <- penguin %>% mutate( sex_island = paste0(island, ": ", sex) ) bar5 <- penguin %>% count(sex_island) %>% ggplot(aes(x = fct_rev(sex_island), y = n, fill = sex_island)) + geom_col() + coord_flip() + scale_fill_manual(values = ncolours$colours_pairs) bar5 ``` ### Pairs ```{r} island_species <- penguin %>% group_by(species, sex) %>% summarise(n = n()) %>% filter(!is.na(sex)) %>% group_by(species) %>% mutate(sex_percent = 100 * (n/ sum(n))) bar4 <- island_species %>% ggplot(aes(x = species, y = sex_percent, fill = sex)) + geom_col(position ="dodge2") + scale_fill_manual(values = ncolours$colours_pairs) + ylim(c(0,100)) bar4 ```
